card.hook: That zigzag roof looks like it was knitted from tiles, and it rises out of one of the busiest squares in Vienna. Good news: the square is open enough that you can step back and fit the whole thing in.
card.stand_here: Stand in Stephansplatz, right in front of the main west entrance. It's about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the building, and you'll be facing the cathedral to the east of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade and roof in one go. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the roof tiles and tower details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and hold your phone upright and level so the towers don't lean, then tap the brightest part of the façade and slide it a touch darker to keep the sky and roof tiles colourful.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the square is quieter and the first light hits the roof tiles. Midday is the busiest time, so expect a crowd then.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Stephansplatz in front of the main entrance, with the façade and tiled roof behind you, and use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) to get the cathedral over your shoulder. For a quieter backdrop, try the narrow Jasomirgottstraße, where the main entrance and the Riesentor are framed at the end of the street.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the far end of the Graben and aim back at the cathedral while you stand in front of it, so the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside the cathedral, and photos in the main nave are for personal use only. Rules can change, so check the cathedral's current ones before you go in. The South Tower climb is paid, so check the official site for tower details.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the zigzag roof tiles, the tall tower and the carved doorway all squeeze into one photo, and see if you can get all three in with nobody's head in the way.
card.good_to_know: The first church on this spot was dedicated in 1147, and the Gothic building you see today grew mainly from work started under Duke Rudolf IV in the 14th century. The south tower, nicknamed the "Steffl", reaches 136 metres. A fire badly damaged the roof in April 1945, and the cathedral fully reopened in 1952.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Stephansplatz, right in front of the main west entrance. It's about 1 minute on foot to the middle of the building, and you'll be facing the cathedral to the east of you.

card.hook: Most people snap Schönbrunn at the front door and go home with a very big yellow wall. The better picture is waiting up the hill, where the whole palace sits in front of you like a model.
card.stand_here: Walk south up through the gardens to the upper terrace of the Gloriette, the colonnaded building on the hill. Then turn round and face back north down the garden axis, with the palace straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the lawns, the palace and the city in one go. If your phone has 2x, use it to pick the palace out from the skyline. Save 0.5x for when you want the terrace's columns or arches in the shot.

card.best_time: Guides disagree, so pick what suits your day: about an hour before sunset for the glow, or early morning to beat the crowds.

For a second option, try the palace-side edge of the Neptune Fountain basin at the foot of the Gloriette hill, with the palace behind you.
card.ask_someone: Try the road outside the main entrance, where the palace exterior can be photographed even when the park gates are closed: hand your phone over and stand with the palace behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed in restricted areas, though the courtyards and gardens are open for non-commercial photography. Photography is not allowed inside the state rooms. Opening hours for the Gloriette terrace can vary, and the Ehrenhof may close for works or events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the palace on the middle vertical line, and sneak a column into one corner. Bonus points if the garden paths point straight at it.
card.good_to_know: Schönbrunn was the Habsburgs' summer palace, and it has 1,441 rooms. It became a World Heritage Site in 1996, together with its gardens. The Gloriette has stood on its hill since 1775, and the hill is about 60 metres high, enough to look down the whole length of the gardens.

card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the archway in the centre, then tap the dome and drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go before 8am, when the square is emptiest. Later it fills up with people and carriages, so a clear frame gets harder.
card.selfie_here: Michaelerplatz, on the semicircular square at the Hofburg's main entrance, is the classic spot. card.challenge: Take a few steps sideways until the dome sits dead centre in the arch, then keep the Roman excavation glass along the bottom edge. Bonus points if you keep the phone perfectly level.
card.good_to_know: The Hofburg was the main palace of the Habsburg dynasty. Since 1946 it has been the official residence and workplace of Austria's president. The oldest parts date from the 13th century, and the Neue Burg was finished between 1881 and 1913.

card.hook: Most people photograph the Vienna State Opera from the pavement, squinting past tram wires. Climb up instead, and the whole pale facade is laid out in front of you like a stage set.

card.best_time: Golden hour or blue hour, when the facade is lit up and the sky turns deep blue. At blue hour, rest your phone against a wall or railing and let night mode do the work.
card.selfie_here: On the Albertina Terrace, stand at the balustrade edge or beside the statue there, with the Opera behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little low so the building fills the background. Try 0.5x if your phone has it on the front camera. For softer light, walk down to the Opera Arcades, the stone walkway beneath the Opera, which guides say suits portraits.

card.rules_and_safety: The Albertina terrace is a public space, so you can stand there without a ticket. Photos and video are not allowed during performances, and flash is not allowed inside the opera house.

card.good_to_know: The opera was the first major building on the Ringstrasse, built between 1861 and 1869. It opened with Mozart's Don Giovanni in May 1869 and seats 1,709 people. A fire in March 1945 destroyed most of the interior, but the front section survived, including the main stairways and the foyer, which is why the facade still looks so complete.

card.hook: Picture a big green dome floating upside down in a shallow pool, with two tall columns standing guard on either side. That's the Karlskirche on a calm day, and your phone will love it.

card.best_time: Go at sunrise, dusk or blue hour, when the water is still and the church is lit up. The reflection only works in the warmer months, when the pool has water in it. Check the columns before you plan your shot, because one was recently reported to be under scaffolding.

Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the church fits over your shoulder. The western edge of Resselpark, the park next to the church, is a second option, with the church in view from the park paths.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the pool's edge on the Resselpark side, facing the church, so the pool, the dome and both columns all fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos without flash are usually allowed inside the church, so follow the signs. Karlsplatz stays well lit and busy in the evening, and one guide calls it a safe place to enjoy the illuminated church after dark.

card.good_to_know: Emperor Charles VI promised to build the church in 1713, a year after the last big plague epidemic in Vienna. He dedicated it to Saint Charles Borromeo, who was revered as a healer of plague sufferers. Building ran from 1716 to 1737, and the two tall columns with spiral reliefs were inspired by Trajan's Column in Rome.

card.hook: Two enormous sandstone twins stare at each other across a leafy square, and you get to stand right between them. The Kunsthistorisches Museum is as much the star as the paintings inside.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits at the Kunsthistorisches Museum itself, at the centre of the building. Face the façade, and if it won't fit, step back towards Maria-Theresien-Platz where there's more room.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the long façade in when you're close, then go to 1x for a natural look. Try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the dome and the carved stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale stonework, then slide it a little darker so the sandstone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stone, and it's likely to be quieter early in the day. In the evening, use night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a wall.
card.selfie_here: Head to Maria-Theresien-Platz by the Maria Theresa monument, turn your back on the museum and use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to squeeze more of the façade over your shoulder. Fancy an indoor one? The domed café hall inside has the cupola and marble behind you, but you'll need a museum ticket.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square near the Maria Theresa monument and shoot towards the museum, while you stand in front of it so the full façade fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is not allowed inside. Guides disagree on whether you can photograph in the galleries, so check the museum's current rules before you go.
card.challenge: Line up the dome on the centre gridline for a perfectly symmetrical shot, then see if you can sneak in a second one of a single row of arched windows with no people in it.
card.good_to_know: The museum was built between 1871 and 1891 to plans by Gottfried Semper and Karl von Hasenauer. Emperor Franz Joseph I commissioned it, along with the near-twin Natural History Museum opposite, to house the Habsburgs' art collection and open it to the public. The dome is about 60 metres high, and inside, the grand stairway is decorated with paintings by Gustav Klimt, Ernst Klimt, Franz Matsch, Hans Makart and Mihály Munkácsy.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits at the Kunsthistorisches Museum itself, at the centre of the building. Face the façade, and if it won't fit, step back towards Maria-Theresien-Platz where there's more room.

card.stand_here: Stand on Linke Wienzeile, on the market side of the street in the mid-section near the antique stalls (the middle of the market lies just to the south-east). Face along the aisle so the stalls spill out in front of you and the Wagner houses rise behind them.

card.best_time: Saturday morning is the busiest and liveliest, with the flea market in full swing next door. Weekday mornings are quieter if you'd like clearer aisles.

card.challenge: Find a pyramid of olives, a hand-written sign and a spice display, and get all three in one photo story.
card.good_to_know: The market started out as the Aschenmarkt, and the name Naschmarkt took over around 1820. The first pavilions over the Wien River went up in 1902. The Saturday flea market along the neighbouring stretch has been going since 1977.

card.hook: Picture a wide, straight street with grand shopfronts lining both sides and your eye running all the way down it. That's the Graben, and it's tailor-made for a phone photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Stephansplatz end of the Graben and look back down the street. The middle of the Graben lies to the west, about 4 minutes on foot (about 250 m), if you want the Plague Column in the foreground later.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to take in the whole street, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. Try zoom 2x to pick out details like the Plague Column or the Hofburg dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the centre of the street on the middle line so the façades balance on both sides.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can, because the street is much emptier then. Watch out for delivery vehicles in the early hours.
card.selfie_here: Stand near where the Graben meets Stephansplatz with the street stretching out behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the street, and for a different shot try standing right in front of the Plague Column and holding the phone low. Nobody gives an exact spot for these, so have a quick test shot and adjust.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back from the Plague Column, toward the shopfronts, while you stand by the column so the whole monument fits in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Graben is a free public street and photos for personal use are generally fine. Just avoid close-up shots of strangers or private property without their okay.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the street's centre line runs straight through the middle of your frame, with the façades balanced on both sides and no wonky walls.
card.good_to_know: Graben means 'ditch'. It goes back to the Roman camp of Vindobona, where a trench ran in front of the settlement wall. The Babenberg dukes filled it in at the end of the 12th century, paid for with the ransom collected for Richard the Lionheart. In 1974 it became Vienna's first pedestrian zone, at first on a provisional basis.

card.stand_here: Stand at the south corner of Kegelgasse and Löwengasse, across the street from the facade. The house is about 1 minute on foot away to the east, so face east with the whole building in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the full facade and the rolling pavement. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for tiles, mirrors and window frames.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the neighbouring buildings straight, then tap a brightly coloured wall and drag the brightness slider a touch darker if the sky is washing out the top.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the tour groups show up around mid-morning. The street is quieter then, so it's much easier to get your shot.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the corner where Löwengasse meets Kegelgasse, facing the building. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it up a little so the wavy colours and greenery fill the space over your shoulder.

card.hook: Vienna's most famous concert hall dresses like a Greek temple, and it looks great on a phone because all those columns are begging to be photographed straight. The only catch is the pedestrians and traffic, so be ready to wait a moment for a clear frame.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full width of the building from close by, then switch to 1x for a more natural look at the front. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the columns and the top of the façade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the columns and rooflines with them, holding the phone upright (tilting it up makes the walls lean inwards).
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight, like a bright overcast day, is kind to the pale stonework, and early in the day there are usually fewer people. In the evening, use night mode and brace the phone against something steady.
card.selfie_here: Go up the front steps on the Musikvereinsplatz side, which a travel guide calls a classic check-in spot. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the neoclassical façade behind you, over your shoulder.

card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the columns perfectly straight on the gridlines, then one close-up of a detail nobody else would bother with.
card.good_to_know: The Musikverein has been home to the Vienna Philharmonic since it opened on 6 January 1870. Emperor Franz Joseph I granted the land during the building of the Ringstraße, and Danish-born architect Theophil Hansen designed it in the style of an ancient Greek temple. Inside is the Golden Hall, known for its acoustics and the annual Vienna New Year's Concert.

card.hook: It looks like it has stood here since the Middle Ages, with its white spires and giant rose window. It's actually a youngster, and people often mix it up with Stephansdom.
card.stand_here: Stand in Votivpark, the park beside the Votive Church on the Ringstraße, and face the front of the church. That puts both spires in one frame with open space around them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're close to a tall building and need both spires to fit. If you walk further back, switch to 1x for a more natural look. Try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for the rose window and the statues above the doorways.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then slide it a touch darker so the white stone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day, when the light is soft, is kinder to pale stone than harsh midday sun, and an evenly cloudy sky works well too. Want magnolia blossom in Sigmund-Freud-Park? Bloom times vary, so check on the day.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the grass at Rooseveltplatz, in front of the church, with the towers rising behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so both spires fit over your shoulder. card.ask_someone: Stand in the street at the far end of Frankgasse, where it runs straight toward the church, and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the church at the end of the view.
card.rules_and_safety: The park and the outside of the church are public space, but the inside is a place of worship, so be respectful during services and check the official site before you go. The front is sometimes covered by advertising banners, so have a look at the facade first.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, line the central doorway up with the middle line, and see if you can get both spires perfectly even on each side.
card.good_to_know: The church was paid for by donations, as a thank-you after Emperor Franz Joseph survived an assassination attempt in 1853. card.hook: Walk up to Vienna City Hall and you'll quickly find your phone can't fit it in. It's about 152 metres long, so you'll end up backing away, and that's exactly the right instinct.

card.zoom: Use zoom 1x from the middle of the square to fit the whole front in. Try zoom 0.5x only if stalls or crowds force you closer, and zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the tower, the Rathausmann and the statues above the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the central tower on the middle line, then tap the sky near the top of the tower and drag the brightness slider down a little so the pale sky doesn't wash out the stonework.

card.selfie_here: Head across the road to the Volksgarten and stand on the park paths or beside the flower beds and benches, with the Rathaus framed through the trees behind you. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if yours has it) and hold the phone a little low and out to the side so the building peeks over your shoulder. card.good_to_know: Vienna City Hall is a Gothic Revival building designed by Friedrich von Schmidt and built between 1872 and 1883. card.hook: Vienna's joke is that Athena turned her back on the Parliament because she got tired of the squabbling inside. Stand in front of her and you'll see why it's such a good photo: she's already posing.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: right in front of the west façade, by the Pallas Athena fountain. Face the building so the statue and fountain figures sit at the bottom of your frame and the columns and roofline fill the rest.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the fountain and façade together. If you're close and the roofline won't fit, tap 0.5x. From the Dr.-Karl-Renner-Ring, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the building with the City Hall tower behind it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the statue on a lower third and keep your phone level so the tall columns stay straight.
card.best_time: Check how the light falls on the façade when you arrive and time your visit to suit. Evening light is lovely for the angled view from the Dr.-Karl-Renner-Ring.
card.selfie_here: Climb the front steps to the eight columns at the main entrance (Dr.-Karl-Renner-Ring 3) and stand under the triangular marble relief. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the building fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: In the Volksgarten, near the rose garden and the Theseus Temple, ask a passer-by to take your photo with the roses and the temple in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Restoration work nearby means scaffolding or fencing may hide parts of the façade, so be ready to change your angle. You can photograph the outside and the fountain from public space, but interior photos and the roof terrace need a guided tour, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get Athena on a lower third with the columns behind her, then ask your friends to guess why she's turned away.
card.good_to_know: The Parliament is where Austria's two houses of parliament meet, and it covers over 13,500 square metres. Theophil Hansen designed it in Greek Revival style because ancient Greece was linked with democracy. The foundation stone was laid in 1874, the building was finished in 1883, and it reopened in 2023 after five years of renovation. Carl Kundmann made the fountain from Hansen's plans between 1898 and 1902.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject: right in front of the west façade, by the Pallas Athena fountain. Face the building so the statue and fountain figures sit at the bottom of your frame and the columns and roofline fill the rest.

card.hook: Tuck into the narrow lane just behind St. Stephen's Cathedral and you're outside the only Viennese home of Mozart that's still standing. He wrote The Marriage of Figaro on the first floor, so this is a good place to say "I was here".
card.stand_here: Stand on Domgasse, in front of the Mozarthaus at number 5. The Mozarthaus facade at Domgasse 5 is just to the north-east, so face that way and you'll see the front of the building with the Old Town lane around it.
card.zoom: The lane is tight, so start at zoom 0.5x and step back as far as you comfortably can to fit the whole front in. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a doorway or window.
card.make_it_pop: Switch the gridlines on and hold your phone upright, lining the building's edges up with the vertical lines so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer on the outside of the building.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Domgasse with the Mozarthaus facade behind you, then use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the building over your shoulder. You can also try the free interactive selfie point in the left-hand window beside the entrance, where a rotating Mozart-face installation sits in front of a Mozart silhouette. It's a fun extra, but it won't show the whole building behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Domgasse opposite the entrance at number 5, with you in front of the door, so the whole entrance front fits in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside the museum may be restricted, so look at the signs and ask staff before you take your phone out.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the whole facade and one close-up of a single window or doorway, then see which one feels more like Mozart's Vienna.
card.good_to_know: Mozart lived here from 1784 to 1787, and it's the only one of his Viennese homes that survives. The building dates from the 17th century and was redeveloped in 1716. Today it's a museum, also known as the Figaro House.

card.hook: Locals just call it "die Burg", and one look from across the Ring tells you why: curved wings, rows of columns, and a whole open square to admire it from. You barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Stand in Rathausplatz, on the Rathausplatz side of the Ring, opposite the Burgtheater. The theatre is to the north-east, about 2 minutes on foot, so face north-east and the whole front is right there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole façade in. If the square is crowded, or you want more open space in front, go to zoom 0.5x. If your phone has zoom 2x, use it for the columns and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the façade with them so the building doesn't lean, then tap the façade and drag the slider a touch darker if the lit front looks glary.
card.best_time: After dark is the favourite, because the façade is lit up. Daytime works well too, as long as the square isn't too busy.
card.selfie_here: Stay in Rathausplatz, stand in the open square facing the Rathaus, and the Burgtheater is right behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the theatre over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the square, where the theatre's front façade and the Ring are both in view, with you standing in the frame in front of the theatre.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the Burgtheater during performances, so keep your photos to the outside. In colder months a winter ice rink on the square may block part of the view.
card.challenge: Get the whole front of the Burgtheater in one frame with the façade perfectly level on the grid, and no stranger's head sneaking in at the bottom.
card.good_to_know: The Burgtheater company began in 1741 under Empress Maria Theresa, in a building beside the Hofburg palace. The theatre you see today opened on the Ringstraße on 14 October 1888, designed by Gottfried Semper and Karl Freiherr von Hasenauer. It was largely destroyed in March 1945 and rebuilt between 1953 and 1955.

card.hook: This theatre is so big that your first photo will probably chop off the roof, and that's the fun of it. It's Vienna's 'people's opera', and it needs a bit of elbow room.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, near Währinger Gürtel, right at the theatre itself. Then walk back across Währinger Straße and turn around to face the front of the building.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x while you're close to the building. Once you're across the street, switch to zoom 1x for a more natural look. For the entrance and the decoration above it, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the building up with a flat line, so the walls stand up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you clear detail on the façade. Early evening is lovely too, when the building is lit and people are arriving for a performance (the season runs September to June).
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, step back across the street and turn so the whole building sits behind you. Try zoom 0.5x if your front camera has it, and hold the phone a bit higher so the façade fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos and recordings aren't permitted during performances, so save the phone for the outside. Watch for traffic when you step back across the street.
card.challenge: Fit the whole façade in with a little street life at the bottom, then take a second shot with a passer-by to show how big it really is.
card.good_to_know: The Volksoper opened in 1898 as a civic theatre for plays and was built in just ten months to mark an imperial jubilee. It took its present name and musical focus in the years after 1903, and today it seats around 1,260 people. Film fans: it appeared in the 1987 James Bond film The Living Daylights, standing in for a conservatory in Bratislava.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon on the map, near Währinger Gürtel, right at the theatre itself. Then walk back across Währinger Straße and turn around to face the front of the building.

card.hook: Here's the fun of the MQ: a grand Baroque frontage sits right next to a plain modern block, and you can get both in one picture. Stand in the middle of it and turn slowly, because every direction gives you a different shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in the MuseumsQuartier about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin, right at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You'll be among the buildings, not looking at them from far away.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full width of a building into the shot. Then switch to 1x, or a little zoom like 2x, for tidier details like windows, rooflines and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the vertical edges of the buildings so they don't lean, and if the sky is bright, tap a building and slide it a touch darker so the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, so you're more likely to get fewer people in your frame. Soft daylight is kinder to the buildings than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the colourful Enzi lounges in the main courtyard and stand beside them (or sit on one) with the MuseumsQuartier buildings behind you. Use the front camera, or switch to 0.5x to squeeze in more of the courtyard. The bright colours pop against the grey pavement.
card.rules_and_safety: Which parts of the MQ are open to walk through and which need a ticket can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find one frame that shows a Baroque building and a modern one side by side, with the gridlines keeping every edge dead straight. Bonus points if nobody walks through it.
card.good_to_know: The MuseumsQuartier covers about 9 hectares in Vienna's 7th district and mixes Baroque buildings with modern architecture by Laurids and Manfred Ortner. The old court stables were renovated from April 1998, and the quarter opened in two stages in June and September 2001. Today it holds the Leopold Museum, MUMOK and the Kunsthalle Wien, plus a children's museum.

card.hook: Most people squeeze into the busy square and point their phone straight up at the Riesenrad. Here's a calmer way: let the chestnut trees on the Hauptallee do the framing for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Hauptallee, the long avenue, at some distance from the wheel, and face north-east. The wheel should sit in the gap between the trunks. Stay on the avenue instead of walking up to the base, because the distance is what makes the framing work.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the trees and the wheel both fit. If the wheel looks small, try 2x or higher (depending on your phone) to bring it closer between the trunks.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the wheel in the middle of the gap with a little sky above it, and keep the phone level so the trees don't lean.
card.best_time: Sunset or dusk is lovely, when the light is soft and the wheel lights up. Use night mode and brace yourself against a tree. Warm evenings and weekends get busy, so go on a weekday if you can.
card.selfie_here: Try Wiener Riesenradplatz, at the foot of the wheel. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and stand with the wheel over your shoulder. For a calmer backdrop, do the same on the Hauptallee with the wheel framed past the trees.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on Prater Allee, about 500 m south of the wheel, and stand a few steps in front of them so the wheel is behind you. It works best at night when the wheel is lit.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules vary by ride, and some rides may not allow phones, so check with the ride operator first. Photographing the wheel from the Hauptallee is free, but riding it is a paid attraction, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few frames and see if you can catch a gondola peeking out between two trunks.
card.good_to_know: The Wiener Riesenrad went up in 1897 to mark Emperor Franz Josef I's Golden Jubilee, and it stands about 65 metres tall. From 1920 until 1985 it was the tallest Ferris wheel still standing anywhere. After wartime damage it was rebuilt with 15 gondolas instead of the original 30, which is why it looks so light and open.
